d.title: Naive Bayes wins, and the baseline is the number that makes any of it meaningful
d.caption: **The majority class gets 0.2583, so every model here is doing real work** — without that row, 0.87 is an unreadable number. And the ordering is the useful surprise: **Naive Bayes at 0.9040 beats both Logistic Regression and SVM on 2,323 training documents.** The cross-validated spread says it is not noise — ±0.0084 against LR's ±0.0156. **On a small, balanced, bag-of-words problem the simplest model is not a concession.**

d.title: One unseen word would have collapsed the whole product
d.caption: **`good` never appears in a negative document, so without smoothing `P(good | c0)` is 0 and the entire product collapses** — the same failure 1.5 measured for n-gram models, and the same fix. With add-one it gets 0.0588 rather than 0, **and class 1 wins by about 1.1 nats**, which sklearn's `MultinomialNB` agrees with. Note the shape of the decision: **a sum of logs, so each word contributes additively and one word can carry the classification.**

d.title: Ninety-eight percent accurate, and it never once predicted the thing you care about
d.caption: A 2% positive rate and a model that always answers negative: **accuracy 0.9800, macro-F1 0.4949, recall on the positive class 0.0000.** The accuracy figure is not slightly misleading, it is **the majority rate with a model-shaped label on it.** Which is why macro-F1 is the usual default on imbalanced data — it averages per class, so a class never predicted drags it down — and why **per-class recall is the metric when one class carries the cost: fraud, disease, abuse.**

d.title: Three options, and the order to try them in is the reverse of the order people try them
d.caption: **The classical baseline trains in under a minute, is interpretable, and is frequently within a few points — so run it first**, because it is also the number that tells you whether anything harder is worth it. A **fine-tuned transformer** is the accuracy answer once you have a few thousand labelled examples: `AutoModelForSequenceClassification` with `num_labels`, learning rate around **2e-5**, two to four epochs. **Zero-shot is for the case where labels do not exist yet** — exploration, a new label tomorrow, a long tail of rare categories — and it is slow per document.

nodes.label: Classical: under a minute to train
nodes.sub: and often within a few points

nodes.label: So it is also your baseline

d.title: Faint praise lands slightly negative, which a word-counter would get wrong
d.caption: VADER's `compound` runs from −1 to +1, and **the third row is the one worth reading: *okay, nothing special* at −0.092 — very slightly negative, which is a reasonable reading of faint praise and something a naive positive-word counter gets wrong** (it would see *okay* and *special* and call it positive). The four approaches split on one axis: **VADER and TextBlob need no training data at all; the other two need labels or a pretrained model.**

d.title: Five rules, and the negation one changes the sign
d.caption: Capitalisation does **nothing** here — `good` and `GOOD` both score +0.440, which is worth knowing because VADER is often described as handling emphasis. What it does handle is measurable: **punctuation lifts +0.440 to +0.583, a booster lifts it to +0.493, and negation flips it to −0.341.** The last row is the strongest: **`bad` at −0.542 becomes `not bad` at +0.431** — a sign change, which is the thing a bag of words structurally cannot do.

d.title: Five sentences, five wrong answers, and each wrong for a different reason
d.caption: **Sarcasm needs world knowledge about meetings. Litotes needs *not bad* to be mild praise rather than negated praise. Comparison needs the model to know which clause is the subject. Unrealised intent needs *wanted to* to reverse *love*. And *unbelievable* is genuinely ambiguous out of context.** No rule list closes these, **because each requires something outside the sentence — which is the argument for a model with context, and the reason §05 ends where it does.**

steps.code: 'The movie was not bad at all.'
'...better than their last, which was awful'

d.title: Domain register beats general accuracy, and the lexicon cannot be fixed
d.caption: **A model trained on movie reviews applied to financial news reads *volatile*, *aggressive* and *exposure* as negative when they are neutral domain terms, and misses that *beat expectations* is strongly positive.** Lexicons are worse still, **because the polarity is fixed at build time** — *sick* is positive in one register and negative in another, and no amount of context helps a static table. **So: assume a general model is wrong on your domain until measured, and budget a few hundred hand-labelled examples to check.**

nodes.label: VADER: social, short, no labels, now
ABSA when the output must be per-aspect
So measure on your own sample first

d.title: Two Dirichlet priors, and they are the two dials you actually set
d.caption: The generative story is short: **draw a topic mixture for the document, draw a topic per word, draw a word from that topic.** The two priors are what put the *latent Dirichlet* in the name, and they are the parameters with an interpretable effect: **low `α` means each document is about one or two topics and high `α` means documents blend many; `β` does the same for how concentrated each topic is over words.** Everything else is inference.

nodes.label: Draw a word from that topic

d.title: Four topics, four real categories, and the mapping is not one-to-one
d.caption: LDA is **not told** the categories and recovers something close to them — but read the purity column rather than the word lists. **Hockey splits into two topics: one about the game at 93% pure, and one that is `pts pt 16 10 vs 25 11`, which is box-score formatting at 81%.** That second one is not a topic anybody wanted; **it is a co-occurrence cluster of numbers, and it is also a correct result.** Meanwhile graphics and guns sit at 58% and 61%, mixing with each other's vocabulary.

d.title: Perplexity keeps falling past the number of real categories
d.caption: There are **four** real categories in this corpus, and perplexity improves monotonically through `k=10` — **4889 at k=2, 4350 at k=4, 3970 at k=10.** So the metric does not have a minimum at the right answer, and **optimising it selects for more topics, not better ones.** Which is the practical point: **`k` is chosen by reading the topics and deciding whether they are useful, with perplexity as a sanity check rather than a criterion.**

d.title: Four methods, and the last one is not a joke
d.caption: NMF is **faster, deterministic and often more coherent on short text**, which matters because LDA's seed-dependence is §05's first point. Embedding clustering is the quality ceiling now and needs an embedding model. **And “just read them” is the honest recommendation under about 1,000 documents** — sampling a few hundred documents gives you the real categories, costs an afternoon, and avoids presenting a word distribution as if it were a finding.

d.title: Topics are word distributions that a human labels
d.caption: **Two runs with different seeds give different topics, and both can be defensible** — so a topic is not a category and should not be reported as one. **Junk topics are normal**: numbers, boilerplate, mailing-list headers and OCR noise co-occur strongly, which is exactly what §02's box-score topic was. **Filter the vocabulary rather than the topics.** And there is **no `k` where every topic is clean** — related categories merge low and fragment high — so **the check worth running is stability: fit several times and see which topics recur.**

nodes.label: A topic is a word distribution
No k is clean: merge low, fragment high
Check stability: refit and see what recurs

d.title: The middle value is 0.151, and the reason is a default nobody mentions
d.caption: The quoted figure is roughly 0.4 and **the measured value is 0.151** — because `TfidfVectorizer` **drops single-character tokens by default**, so `I` is not a feature and the two documents share only `learning`. Which is the lesson in miniature: **a similarity number is a property of the vectoriser's settings as much as of the text.** The third row is the one that matters either way: **two documents sharing no words score exactly 0, whatever they mean.**

steps.code: 'I love machine learning' / 'I enjoy deep learning'

d.title: Paraphrase scores 0.000 and an unrelated pair scores 0.311
d.caption: Read the first and last rows together, because together they are the whole indictment. **A genuine paraphrase — *how to learn machine learning* against *the best way to study ML* — scores exactly 0.000, because it shares no words.** And *the bank raised rates* against *the river bank was muddy* scores **0.311, the highest in the table**, because it shares `the` and `bank`. **The ranking is not merely noisy: it is inverted on the two cases that matter most.**

d.title: The same four pairs, and the ordering is now right
d.caption: 384 dimensions and the inversion is gone: **the synonym pair goes 0.247 to 0.910, the paraphrase 0.155 to 0.737, and the ML question pair 0.000 to 0.534.** Note the honest detail: **the reference quotes ~0.85 for that last pair and the measured value is 0.534** — so a short embedding model is less confident on a paraphrase with no shared vocabulary than the write-up suggests. **The ordering is what you rely on, not the magnitude.**

d.title: Exact cosine is one dot product per document, per query
d.caption: The arithmetic is unforgiving because it is linear in corpus size and there is no constant factor to hide in: **at 10 million documents and 384 dimensions, one query is 3.8×10⁹ multiply-adds.** Which is why approximate nearest-neighbour indexes exist at all — **not to make the search smarter, but to stop it being a full scan.** And the cost is per **query**, so it is paid at serving time rather than once at build time.

d.title: Five tasks that are one task
d.caption: **All of these assign one label per token and decode spans from the label sequence — so the same model, the same BIO scheme and the same decoding algorithm serve all of them.** Which is why sequence labelling is worth treating as a single topic rather than learning NER and POS tagging separately: **the only thing that changes between the rows is the label set**, and POS tagging is the degenerate case where spans are always one token long.

items.label: POS tagging
items.sub: one tag per token, no spans

items.label: Chunking
items.sub: flat phrase boundaries, no full parse

d.title: A 0.1 preference at one token produces an invalid tag sequence
d.caption: These are raw per-token scores, before any structure is imposed. **At *Steve* the model prefers `I-PER` at 1.50 over `B-PER` at 1.40 — a difference of 0.1, well inside the noise of any real model** — and greedy decoding takes it, emitting `O → I-PER`, which 1.7 showed decodes to nothing. **So the failure is not a weak model: the scores are fine, and argmax-per-token has no way to know that a tag sequence can be structurally invalid.**

d.title: Exact, not a heuristic, and 10^157 sequences become 136,900 updates
d.caption: Each cell holds **the best score of any path ending in that tag**, so the invalid `O → I-PER` move is scored at −∞ rather than pruned — **no valid path is ever discarded, which is why Viterbi is exact and not a search heuristic.** The result flips the decode: **`O B-PER I-PER O` at 8.80 against greedy's path at −999999991.70.** And the cost is `O(T·K²)` against `O(K^T)` — **at 100 tokens and 37 tags, 136,900 cell updates against 10^157 sequences.**

d.title: An intent and its arguments, which is sequence labelling plus one classification
d.caption: *“Book a flight from New York to London on Friday”* gives **one intent and three slots** — and the decomposition is the point: **the intent is a sentence-level classification (2.1) and the slots are span extraction (1.7), running over the same tokens.** Which is why a slot-filling model is usually one encoder with two heads rather than two models: the features that tell you this is a `book_flight` request are the features that tell you `London` is the destination.

nodes.label: So: one encoder, two heads
nodes.sub: the features are the same features

d.title: One argument does the span decoding, and without it you are back in 1.7's alignment trap
d.caption: `aggregation_strategy="simple"` turns per-subword tags into merged spans with scores — **without it you get per-subword tags and have to merge them yourself, which is exactly where 1.7's alignment trap lives.** And the modern default is simpler than the lesson implies: **a transformer encoder alone is usually enough, because the contextual representation makes most invalid transitions unlikely even without a CRF.** The CRF earns its place when **the output must be structurally valid by construction**, or the tag scheme has hard constraints the data does not fully teach.

nodes.label: Add a CRF when validity must be guaranteed
Or when the data under-teaches the scheme
